input: It is important to note that phase equilibrium is a truly fundamental concept in the study of mixtures, serving as the cornerstone for understanding how different phases coexist and interact within a system. In essence, when a binary mixture is held at a fixed pressure, equilibrium is governed by an elegant and powerful condition: the chemical potential of each and every component must be equal across all of the phases in which that component is present, ensuring that the system rests in a stable and balanced state. This essentially means that no component can gain anything by moving from one phase to another, and it is this delicate balance that ultimately defines the equilibrium state of the mixture as a whole. Consider, for example, a liquid mixture in contact with its own vapour at a fixed pressure. Interestingly, the liquid and the vapour do not share the same composition; rather, the more volatile component is enriched in the vapour phase, highlighting the selective and preferential nature of the transfer process. Furthermore, temperature is not an independent quantity in this particular setting: at fixed pressure, once the liquid composition has been specified, the boiling temperature is determined, and the vapour composition follows accordingly, underscoring the tightly coupled and interdependent nature of these variables. When the chemical potentials are not equal, a driving force exists that moves material between the phases, and this transfer continues until the potentials become equal and the system settles into equilibrium, reflecting the deeper tendency of the mixture to seek its lowest-energy configuration.
target: Phase equilibrium in a binary mixture at fixed pressure rests on one condition: at equilibrium, the chemical potential of each component is the same in every phase in which that component is present. The condition is stated in words because it is the definition from which the working relations come. A mixture is at equilibrium when no component can lower the total Gibbs energy by passing from one phase to another, and equality of chemical potential states that condition for each component separately. Consider a liquid mixture in contact with its vapour at a fixed pressure. The liquid has a composition and the vapour has a composition, and the two compositions differ: the more volatile component is richer in the vapour than in the liquid. Temperature is not free once the pressure and one composition are set. At fixed pressure, a binary mixture in two phases has one remaining degree of freedom, so the temperature of the boiling mixture is fixed by its liquid composition; change the liquid composition and the boiling temperature changes with it, and the vapour composition changes as well. Equilibrium is a relation among temperature and the two compositions at the stated pressure, not a property of either phase alone. Away from equilibrium, the chemical potential of a component differs between the phases, and the difference drives transfer of that component from the phase where its chemical potential is higher to the phase where it is lower, until the potentials meet and net transfer stops. The same condition governs condensation; only the direction of transfer reverses.
